reason: Classic science concepts (Kepler's laws, chromosomes, Pasteur, etc.) anchored to their discoverer/theorist's lifespan by bulk extractor but not era-specific.

nodes.label: Dobereiner's Triads
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Johann Wolfgang Dobereiner (1817) grouped elements with similar properties into sets of three (triads). In each triad arranged by increasing atomic mass, the middle element's atomic mass was roughly the average of the other two. Example: Li (6.9), Na (23), K (39). Could identify only three triads from known elements, so the system was not widely useful.

nodes.label: Heredity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The transmission of traits from parents to offspring through genetic material (DNA). Both parents contribute equal amounts of genetic material to the child. Each trait has two versions (alleles) in sexually reproducing organisms, one from each parent. Heredity determines both similarities and variations between generations.

nodes.label: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Gregor Mendel (1822-1884) used pea plants to discover fundamental laws of inheritance. Law of Dominance: in a heterozygous organism, only one trait (dominant) is expressed while the other (recessive) is hidden. Law of Segregation: F2 generation shows 3:1 phenotypic ratio (e.g., tall:short). Law of Independent Assortment: traits are inherited independently, producing new combinations in F2 (e.g., tall-round, tall-wrinkled, short-round, short-wrinkled).

nodes.label: Dominant and Recessive Traits
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A single copy of the dominant allele (e.g., T for tallness) is sufficient for trait expression, while both copies must be recessive (e.g., tt) for the recessive trait to appear. In Mendel's experiments, tallness was dominant over shortness, round seeds over wrinkled, violet flowers over white. F1 generation shows only dominant traits; F2 shows 3:1 ratio.

nodes.label: Genes and Chromosomes
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A gene is a section of DNA that provides information for one protein. Genes control traits through protein (enzyme) production. Chromosomes are independent pieces of DNA; each cell has two copies of each chromosome (one from each parent). Germ cells have only one set of chromosomes, which is restored to the normal number upon fertilization.

nodes.label: Sex Determination
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In humans, sex is genetically determined by sex chromosomes. Women are XX and men are XY. All children inherit an X chromosome from their mother. The sex of the child depends on whether the father contributes an X (girl) or Y (boy) chromosome. Some organisms use environmental cues (e.g., temperature in some reptiles), and some like snails can change sex.

nodes.label: Natural Selection
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process by which organisms with advantageous variations survive and reproduce more successfully. Charles Darwin (1809-1882) proposed this theory after his 5-year voyage to South America. Example: green beetles on green leaves survive predation by crows better than red beetles, so green trait becomes common. Natural selection directs evolution by selecting for fitness advantages.

nodes.label: Genetic Drift
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Random changes in gene frequency in a population, especially significant in small populations. Unlike natural selection, genetic drift does not require a survival advantage. Example: if an elephant accidentally kills most red beetles, surviving blue beetles (by chance) dominate the population. Provides diversity without adaptation. Small tiger populations are at risk due to genetic drift reducing genetic variation.

nodes.label: Speciation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The formation of new species when a population splits into groups that can no longer interbreed. Geographical isolation (e.g., a river forming between populations) reduces gene flow. Over generations, genetic drift and differential natural selection accumulate different changes in isolated sub-populations. Eventually, DNA changes become severe enough (e.g., changed chromosome number) to prevent reproduction between groups.

nodes.label: Homologous Organs
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organs with similar basic structure but different functions, indicating common ancestry. Examples: forelimbs of mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians share the same skeletal structure but are modified for different uses (grasping, flying, walking, swimming). Homologous characteristics are key evidence for tracing evolutionary relationships between apparently different species.

nodes.label: Analogous Organs
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organs that have similar functions but different structural origins, arising from convergent evolution rather than common ancestry. Example: wings of birds (feathery covering along the arm) and wings of bats (skin folds between elongated fingers) look similar for flying but have very different designs. Wings of butterflies and birds are also analogous.

nodes.label: Evolution is Not Progress
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Evolution is the generation of diversity shaped by environmental selection, not a ladder from 'lower' to 'higher' forms. Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; both share a common ancestor. Simpler organisms like bacteria still thrive in extreme habitats (hot springs, deep-sea vents, Antarctic ice). More complex body designs have emerged over time, but older designs remain efficient.

nodes.label: Charles Darwin
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: English naturalist (1809-1882) who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. Undertook a 5-year voyage to South America and offshore islands at age 22, which formed the basis of his theory. Never left England again after returning. Also studied earthworms' role in soil fertility. Contemporary of Mendel but neither knew of the other's work.

nodes.label: Electric Current
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The flow of electricity through a circuit. Current flows from the positive terminal of a cell through the circuit to the negative terminal. A complete circuit is necessary for current to flow. Current makes devices like bulbs and motors work.

nodes.label: Electric Potential Difference
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The work done to move a unit charge from one point to another in an electric circuit (V = W/Q). SI unit is volt (V), named after Alessandro Volta. 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. A cell or battery creates potential difference through chemical energy. Measured using a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component.

nodes.label: Ohm's Law
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Discovered by Georg Simon Ohm (1827): the potential difference across a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current through it, at constant temperature (V = IR). R is resistance in ohms. The V-I graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance depends on length (directly proportional), cross-sectional area (inversely proportional), material (resistivity), and temperature.

nodes.label: Resistance and Resistivity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Resistance (R = rho * l / A) depends on length, cross-section area, and material. Resistivity (rho) is a characteristic property of the material, measured in ohm-metre. Metals have low resistivity (10^-8 to 10^-6 ohm-m); insulators like rubber have very high resistivity (10^12 to 10^17 ohm-m). Alloys have higher resistivity than constituent metals and don't oxidise easily, so they are used in heating devices. Tungsten is used for bulb filaments (melting point 3380 degrees C).

nodes.label: Joule's Law of Heating
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Heat produced in a resistor: H = I^2 * R * t. Heat is proportional to the square of current, the resistance, and the time. Applied in electric heaters, irons, toasters, ovens, and electric bulbs. Bulb filaments use tungsten (high melting point), filled with inert gases (nitrogen, argon) to prolong filament life. Fuses use this principle for safety, melting at high current to break the circuit.

nodes.label: Electric Power
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The rate of energy consumption in an electric circuit: P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R. SI unit is watt (W). 1 watt = 1 volt x 1 ampere. Commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt hour (kWh or 'unit'): 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 joules. Domestic circuits use parallel connections so each appliance gets the same voltage (220V in India) and can be switched independently. Fuse ratings: 1A, 2A, 3A, 5A, 10A etc.

nodes.label: Electromagnetism
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Electricity and magnetism are linked phenomena. Hans Christian Oersted (1820) discovered that a compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire, proving electric current produces a magnetic field. The field around a straight conductor forms concentric circles (direction given by right-hand thumb rule). A solenoid (coil of many circular turns) produces a magnetic field similar to a bar magnet.

nodes.label: Electromagnet
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A core of soft iron wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire. When current flows, the solenoid magnetises the soft iron core, creating a strong magnetic field. The field strength depends on current and number of turns. Electromagnets can be turned on/off unlike permanent magnets, making them useful in electric bells, cranes for lifting heavy iron objects, and MRI machines.

nodes.label: Electric Motor
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Principle: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (Fleming's left-hand rule determines force direction). Key components: rectangular coil (armature with soft iron core), permanent magnet, split-ring commutator (reverses current every half rotation for continuous rotation), and brushes. Used in fans, washing machines, mixers, electric cars.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic Induction
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Discovered by Michael Faraday (1831): a changing magnetic field in a conductor induces an electric current. Current is induced when a magnet moves relative to a coil, or when current in a nearby coil changes. No current flows when magnet and coil are stationary relative to each other. Direction of induced current given by Fleming's right-hand rule. This is the principle behind electric generators.

nodes.label: Electric Generator
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A rotating rectangular coil between magnetic poles induces alternating current (AC). AC generators use slip rings; DC generators use split-ring commutators. In India, AC supply is 220V at 50 Hz (direction changes every 1/100 second). AC is preferred for power transmission as it can be transmitted over long distances with less energy loss.

nodes.label: Domestic Electric Circuits
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Home circuits use three wires: live (red, positive), neutral (black, negative), and earth (green, safety). Potential difference is 220V in India. Two circuits: 15A rating (geysers, air coolers) and 5A rating (bulbs, fans). Appliances are connected in parallel for equal voltage. Safety measures: fuse (melts at high current to break circuit), earth wire (prevents electric shock by grounding metallic bodies). Short-circuiting occurs when live and neutral wires touch directly.

nodes.label: Sacred Groves
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forest tracts set aside by religious and cultural traditions where all trees and wildlife are venerated and given total protection. Found in Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghat regions (Karnataka, Maharashtra), and Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas (Madhya Pradesh). In Meghalaya, sacred groves serve as last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants. Represent India's traditional approach to in situ conservation.

nodes.label: Dominance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In a heterozygous pair, the dominant allele expresses while the recessive is masked. Dominant allele typically produces normal/functional enzyme; recessive produces non-functional or no enzyme. Explained through gene function: normal allele produces sufficient enzyme to transform substrate, so heterozygote shows dominant phenotype. Capital letters denote dominant alleles (T for tall), lowercase for recessive (t for dwarf). Homozygous dominant (TT) and heterozygous (Tt) show same phenotype.

nodes.label: Incomplete Dominance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: F1 phenotype is intermediate between two parents, neither allele fully dominant. Example: snapdragon (Antirrhinum) flower colour - Red (RR) x White (rr) gives Pink (Rr) in F1. F2 ratio is 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White (1:2:1), where phenotypic ratio equals genotypic ratio. Unlike complete dominance, the heterozygote is distinguishable from both homozygotes.

nodes.label: Co-dominance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Both alleles in a heterozygote express equally without blending. Best example: ABO blood grouping in humans. Gene I has three alleles: I^A, I^B, and i. I^A and I^B are co-dominant (both express their sugars when together, producing AB blood group). Both are completely dominant over i. Six genotypes possible but only four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O). Also an example of multiple alleles (more than two alleles for a gene, though each individual carries only two).

nodes.label: ABO Blood Group System
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Controlled by gene I with three alleles: I^A, I^B, i. Red blood cell surface has sugar polymers. I^A produces type A sugar, I^B produces type B sugar, i produces no sugar. Genotypes and phenotypes: I^A I^A or I^A i = Blood Group A; I^B I^B or I^B i = Blood Group B; I^A I^B = Blood Group AB (co-dominance); ii = Blood Group O. Six possible genotypes, four phenotypes. Classic example of both co-dominance and multiple alleles in UPSC questions.

nodes.label: Sex-Linked Inheritance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Genes located on sex chromosomes show sex-linked inheritance patterns. X-linked recessive traits are more common in males (who have only one X). Colour blindness: X-linked recessive, affects ~8% males but only ~0.4% females. A carrier mother has 50% chance of colour-blind son. Haemophilia: X-linked recessive, affects blood clotting cascade proteins. Carrier females transmit to sons. Female haemophilic extremely rare (mother must be carrier, father haemophilic). Queen Victoria was a famous carrier.

nodes.label: Polygenic Inheritance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Traits controlled by three or more genes showing continuous variation rather than discrete alternatives. Effect of each allele is additive. Examples: human skin colour (controlled by genes A, B, C; AABBCC = darkest, aabbcc = lightest), human height. Environmental influence also plays a role. Differs from Mendelian traits which show distinct alternate forms.

nodes.label: Sickle-Cell Anaemia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Autosomal recessive disease caused by point mutation in beta-globin gene. Single base substitution (GAG to GUG) at 6th codon causes glutamic acid to valine substitution. Controlled by alleles Hb^A and Hb^S. Only Hb^S Hb^S homozygotes show disease; Hb^A Hb^S heterozygotes are carriers (sickle-cell trait). Mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen, changing RBC shape from biconcave disc to sickle shape. Classic example of point mutation in UPSC context.

nodes.label: Chipko Movement and Bishnoi Community
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bishnoi community: known for peaceful co-existence with nature. In 1731, when king of Jodhpur ordered tree-felling near Bishnoi village, Amrita Devi hugged a tree, daring men to cut her first. She, her three daughters, and hundreds of Bishnois sacrificed their lives to protect trees. Government instituted Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award. Chipko Movement (1974): women of Garhwal Himalayas protected trees by hugging them against contractors' axes. Globally acclaimed people's movement.

nodes.label: Electric Cell
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A device that produces electricity from chemicals stored inside it. It has two terminals -- positive (+) and negative (-). Cells are used in torches, clocks, radios, and remote controls. When chemicals are used up, the cell stops working.

nodes.label: Electric Circuit
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A complete path through which electric current flows, from one terminal of a cell through a device (like a bulb) and back to the other terminal. A break in the circuit stops the current flow. The circuit must be closed for current to flow.

nodes.label: Electric Bulb
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A device that produces light when electric current flows through it. Inside, a thin wire called the filament gets heated and glows. The bulb has two terminals connecting to the filament. The filament is usually made of tungsten.

nodes.label: Electric Switch
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A device that either completes or breaks an electric circuit. When the switch is 'on', the circuit is complete and current flows. When 'off', there is a gap in the circuit. Switches allow us to control when devices operate.

nodes.label: Electrical Conductor
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Materials that allow electric current to pass through them. Most metals like iron, copper, and aluminium are good conductors. The human body and water (especially impure) are also conductors. Conductors are used to make wires and circuits.

nodes.label: Electrical Insulator
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Materials that do not allow electric current to pass through them. Examples include rubber, plastic, wood, glass, and air. Insulators are used to cover wires and protect people from electric shocks.

nodes.label: Filament
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A thin wire inside an electric bulb that glows when electric current flows through it, producing light. Made of a material with high melting point like tungsten. If the filament breaks, the circuit is broken and the bulb is said to be fused.

nodes.label: Torch (Flashlight)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A portable device that uses cells, a switch, and a bulb to produce light. Contains cells connected in series, a reflector behind the bulb, and a sliding switch. Demonstrates the basic principles of an electric circuit in a practical application.

nodes.label: Electrical Safety
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Since the human body is a conductor, touching exposed wires or faulty electrical equipment can cause electric shock. Insulators like rubber and plastic are used to cover wires. One should never touch electrical appliances with wet hands.

nodes.label: Wool
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An animal fibre obtained from the fleece (hairy skin) of sheep, goat, yak, and some other animals. Sheep are selectively bred for quality wool. Major wool-producing states in India include Rajasthan, Jammu & Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh.

nodes.label: Wool Processing
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Steps include shearing (removing fleece), scouring (washing to remove grease), sorting (separating by texture), dyeing, and spinning into yarn. Shearing is done in summer when sheep do not need the thick coat. The fleece regrows naturally.

nodes.label: Silk
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An animal fibre obtained from the cocoon of the silkworm (caterpillar of silk moth). Silk is known for its lustre and softness. India and China are major silk producers. Different types include mulberry silk, tassar silk, eri silk, and muga silk.

nodes.label: Sericulture
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The rearing of silkworms for obtaining silk. Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves. The caterpillar spins a cocoon of silk fibre around itself. Cocoons are processed by boiling to obtain silk threads. India produces several varieties of silk.

nodes.label: Silk Moth Life Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The life cycle of a silk moth: female moth lays eggs, eggs hatch into caterpillars (silkworms/larvae), caterpillars eat mulberry leaves and grow, then spin cocoons (pupa stage), and finally emerge as adult moths. The cocoon is the source of silk fibre.

nodes.label: Silkworm
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The caterpillar (larva) of the silk moth that produces silk fibre. It feeds on mulberry leaves and secretes silk protein from its salivary glands. A single cocoon can yield up to 1000 metres of silk thread. The silkworm is actually not a worm but a caterpillar.

nodes.label: Pashmina Wool
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A very fine and warm type of wool obtained from pashmina goats found in Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. Pashmina shawls are world-famous for their quality and softness. It is one of the most expensive natural fibres.

nodes.label: Angora Wool
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Soft wool obtained from Angora goats found in hilly regions like Jammu & Kashmir. Angora rabbits also provide very fine, soft fibre. The fibre is valued for its warmth and softness.

nodes.label: Sheep Breeds for Wool
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Different breeds provide different quality wool. Lohi and Nali breeds are from Rajasthan and Punjab. Rampur bushair is from Himachal Pradesh. Bakharwal is from Jammu & Kashmir. Selective breeding has improved wool quality over generations.

nodes.label: Occupational Hazards in Wool Industry
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Workers in the wool industry risk sorter's disease caused by anthrax bacteria (Bacillus anthracis) present in animal fleece. This highlights the occupational health risks in animal fibre industries.

nodes.label: Reeling of Silk
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process of unwinding silk fibres from cocoons. Cocoons are first boiled in water to soften the silk protein and kill the pupa. Then threads from several cocoons are combined and reeled onto spools. This produces raw silk.

nodes.label: Aerobic Respiration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Respiration that occurs in the presence of oxygen. Glucose is completely broken down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy. Most organisms including humans perform aerobic respiration.

nodes.label: Anaerobic Respiration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Respiration that occurs without oxygen. Glucose is partially broken down, releasing less energy. In yeast, it produces alcohol and CO2 (fermentation). In muscles during vigorous exercise, it produces lactic acid causing cramps.

nodes.label: Fermentation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Anaerobic respiration in yeast that converts glucose into alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide. Used in making bread (CO2 causes dough to rise), wine, beer, and idli/dosa batter. Louis Pasteur discovered fermentation in 1857.

nodes.label: Breathing Rate
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The number of times a person breathes per minute. Normal rate is 15-18 breaths per minute in adults. Increases during exercise because muscles need more energy, requiring more oxygen. Also increases at high altitudes where oxygen is scarce.

nodes.label: Respiration in Plants
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plants also respire, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide through stomata. Plant respiration occurs continuously (day and night), unlike photosynthesis which only happens during the day. During the day, the rate of photosynthesis exceeds respiration.

nodes.label: Magnetic Effect of Current
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: When electric current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around it. Discovered by Hans Christian Oersted. A current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle. This property is used to make electromagnets, motors, and generators.

nodes.label: Electric Bell
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A device that uses an electromagnet to produce sound. When current flows, the electromagnet attracts an iron strip that strikes the gong. The circuit then breaks, electromagnet releases the strip, and the cycle repeats rapidly producing ringing.

nodes.label: Circuit Symbols and Diagrams
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Standardised symbols are used to represent components in circuit diagrams: straight lines for wires, specific symbols for cell, battery, bulb, switch, fuse, etc. Circuit diagrams simplify the representation and understanding of electrical circuits.

nodes.label: Microorganisms
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tiny living organisms not visible to the unaided eye, found in all environments from ice cold climates to hot springs. Classified into four major groups: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and algae. They can be unicellular or multicellular and play vital roles in food production, medicine, and ecology.

nodes.label: Protozoa
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Single-celled eukaryotic microorganisms including Amoeba and Paramecium. The protozoan Plasmodium causes malaria and is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Other protozoans cause diseases like dysentery and kala-azar.

nodes.label: Vaccine
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Dead or weakened microbes introduced into a healthy body to stimulate antibody production, providing lasting immunity. Edward Jenner discovered the smallpox vaccine in 1798. Vaccines prevent diseases including cholera, tuberculosis, smallpox, hepatitis, and polio.

nodes.label: Pasteurisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A food preservation process discovered by Louis Pasteur where milk is heated to about 70 degrees Celsius for 15-30 seconds and then suddenly chilled. This kills harmful microbes without significantly altering the food's nutritional value, allowing milk to be consumed without boiling.

nodes.label: Pathogens
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Disease-causing microorganisms that enter the body through air, water, food, or physical contact. They cause communicable diseases that spread from infected to healthy persons. Examples include bacteria causing TB and typhoid, viruses causing polio and chicken pox, and protozoa causing malaria.

nodes.label: Food Preservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Methods to prevent food spoilage by microorganisms. Chemical methods use salt, sugar, oil, vinegar, and preservatives like sodium benzoate. Physical methods include boiling, refrigeration (cold treatment), and pasteurisation. Modern methods include sealed airtight packaging.

nodes.label: Louis Pasteur
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: French scientist who discovered fermentation in 1857 and developed the process of pasteurisation for preserving milk and other foods. His work established the germ theory of disease and laid foundations for microbiology, immunology, and food safety science.

nodes.label: Coal Gas
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A gaseous fuel obtained during the processing of coal to get coke. First used for street lighting in London in 1810 and New York around 1820. Now used as a source of heat in industries situated near coal processing plants.

nodes.label: Chromosomes
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Thread-like structures found in the nucleus that carry genes and help in inheritance or transfer of characters from parents to offspring. Visible only when the cell divides. They are the physical carriers of genetic information in all living organisms.

nodes.label: Prokaryotic Cell
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cells without a well-organised nucleus, lacking a nuclear membrane. The nuclear material is present but not enclosed. Found in bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). The term comes from pro (primitive) and karyon (nucleus). Generally smaller (1-10 micrometres).

nodes.label: Zygote
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The fertilised egg formed by the fusion of sperm and ovum nuclei. It is the beginning of a new individual. The zygote divides repeatedly to give rise to a ball of cells which then develops into an embryo with differentiated tissues and organs.

nodes.label: Embryo
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The developing structure formed from repeated division of the zygote. Cells form groups that develop into different tissues and organs. In humans, it gets embedded in the wall of the uterus for further development and gradually develops body parts.

nodes.label: Foetus
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The stage of the embryo in which all body parts (hands, legs, head, eyes, ears) can be identified. When development of the foetus is complete, the mother gives birth. In hens, the embryo develops inside the egg shell for about 3 weeks before the chick hatches.

nodes.label: Atom
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The smallest particle of an element that maintains its chemical identity. The idea of indivisible particles was proposed by Indian philosopher Maharishi Kanad (as Parmanu) and Greek philosopher Democritus around 500 BC. Dalton's atomic theory (1808) provided the first scientific framework for atoms.

nodes.label: Molecule
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently and shows all properties of that substance. Molecules of elements contain atoms of the same type (O2, N2). Molecules of compounds contain atoms of different elements (H2O, CO2).

nodes.label: Law of Conservation of Mass
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Established by Antoine Lavoisier. The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. This fundamental law laid the foundation of chemical sciences.

nodes.label: Law of Constant Proportions
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In a chemical compound, elements are always present in definite proportions by mass regardless of the source or method of preparation. Established by Joseph Proust. For example, water always has hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:8 by mass.

nodes.label: Dalton's Atomic Theory
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: John Dalton proposed in 1808 that all matter is made of indivisible atoms, atoms of a given element are identical, atoms cannot be created or destroyed, and compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in fixed ratios. Some postulates were later modified.

nodes.label: Atomic Mass Unit
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A unit of mass defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom, used for expressing atomic and molecular masses. Symbol: u. Hydrogen has atomic mass 1u, carbon 12u, oxygen 16u. Relative atomic masses were initially determined relative to hydrogen.

nodes.label: Chemical Formula
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A symbolic representation of a compound showing the types and numbers of atoms present. Water is H2O, carbon dioxide is CO2, sodium chloride is NaCl. The formula is written using valency (combining capacity) of elements following the criss-cross method.

nodes.label: Valency
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The combining capacity of an element, determined by the number of bonds it can form. Hydrogen has valency 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3, and carbon 4. Valency is used to write the chemical formulae of compounds by balancing the combining capacities of constituent elements.

nodes.label: Ion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An atom or group of atoms carrying a positive or negative charge. Cations are positively charged (Na+, Ca2+) and anions are negatively charged (Cl-, SO42-). Polyatomic ions are groups of atoms carrying charge, like hydroxide (OH-), carbonate (CO32-), and ammonium (NH4+).

nodes.label: Mole Concept
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). The molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, numerically equal to its atomic or molecular mass in grams. Provides a link between the microscopic world of atoms and the macroscopic world of measurable quantities.

nodes.label: Antoine Lavoisier
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: French chemist who laid the foundation of chemical sciences by establishing the law of conservation of mass and the law of constant proportions (with Proust). Often called the father of modern chemistry for his systematic approach to chemical experimentation.

nodes.label: Maharishi Kanad
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ancient Indian philosopher (circa 500 BC) who postulated that matter, if continuously divided, would yield the smallest indivisible particles called Parmanu. This was one of the earliest atomistic theories in the world, developed independently of Greek philosophers.

nodes.label: Molecular Mass
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule of a substance. For example, water (H2O) has molecular mass = 2(1) + 16 = 18 u. Formula unit mass is used for ionic compounds like NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

nodes.label: Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A large network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets in the cytoplasm. Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes and manufactures proteins. Smooth ER (SER) manufactures lipids. ER serves as a transport channel, provides cytoplasmic framework, and helps in membrane biogenesis.

nodes.label: Lysosome
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Membrane-bound sacs filled with powerful digestive enzymes made by RER. Called the waste disposal system of the cell, they digest foreign materials, worn-out organelles, and bacteria. During cell damage, they burst and digest the cell itself, earning the name suicide bags.

nodes.label: Ribosome
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Non-membrane bound organelles present in all active cells, found either freely in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum (making it rough ER). They are the sites of protein synthesis, translating genetic information from mRNA into functional proteins.

nodes.label: Universal Law of Gravitation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Every object attracts every other object with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. F = G(m1*m2)/r^2, where G is the universal gravitational constant (6.673 x 10^-11 Nm^2/kg^2).

nodes.label: Gravitational Constant (G)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The universal gravitational constant with value 6.673 x 10^-11 Nm^2/kg^2. Measured by Henry Cavendish in 1798 using a sensitive balance. Its extremely small value explains why gravitational force between everyday objects is negligible.

nodes.label: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Three laws describing planetary orbits: (1) Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus, (2) A line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal time intervals, (3) The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Newton's gravitation explains these laws.

nodes.label: Power
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The rate of doing work or the rate of energy transfer. P = W/t (work divided by time). SI unit is watt (W), where 1 watt = 1 joule per second. Commercial unit is kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. The unit of electricity billing.

nodes.label: Watt
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The SI unit of power, named after James Watt. 1 watt = 1 joule per second. A 40-watt bulb consumes 40 joules of electrical energy per second. Larger units: kilowatt (kW = 1000 W), megawatt (MW = 10^6 W), and horsepower (1 hp ≈ 746 W).

nodes.label: Commercial Unit of Energy (kWh)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The kilowatt-hour (kWh), commonly called a unit of electricity. 1 kWh = 1000 watts x 3600 seconds = 3.6 x 10^6 joules. Electricity bills are calculated based on kWh consumed. The joule is too small for commercial energy measurements.
